title: Styling in React — className, CSS Modules, and cn()

subChunks.title: Styling in React — className, CSS Modules, and cn()
subChunks.hookHtml: React doesn't mandate a styling approach — but it does change how you think about it. Classes are dynamic strings built from your component's state. Styles live close to the components they describe. And the same rules that make components composable make styles composable too. Three tools cover 95% of real-world React styling: plain className, CSS Modules, and the cn() utility.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
className and dynamic classes

In JSX, className is just a prop — which means you can make it dynamic with any JavaScript expression:

// Static class
<div className="card">…</div>

// Dynamic class based on state
<div className={isActive ? 'card card--active' : 'card'}>…</div>

// Template literal for multiple conditions
<div className={`card ${isActive ? 'card--active' : ''} ${hasError ? 'card--error' : ''}`}>
  …
</div>

Template literals get messy fast. That's what cn() solves.

CSS Modules — scoped styles

Name your file Component.module.css and import it as an object. The build tool generates unique class names so styles never leak between components:

/* Card.module.css */
.card {
  border: 1px solid #e2e8f0;
  border-radius: 8px;
  padding: 16px;
}

.active {
  border-color: var(--accent);
  box-shadow: 0 0 0 3px var(--accent-faint);
}
// Card.jsx
import styles from './Card.module.css';

function Card({ isActive, children }) {
  return (
    <div className={`${styles.card} ${isActive ? styles.active : ''}`}>
      {children}
    </div>
  );
}

The generated class name is something like Card_card__x8Kp2 — unique, impossible to collide.

The cn() utility — conditional classes made clean

cn() (from the clsx or classnames package, or hand-rolled) takes any mix of strings, objects, and arrays and merges them into one class string:

import { cn } from '@/lib/utils'; // common pattern in shadcn/ui projects

function Button({ variant = 'primary', disabled, children }) {
  return (
    <button
      className={cn(
        'btn',                          // always applied
        variant === 'primary' && 'btn-primary',
        variant === 'secondary' && 'btn-secondary',
        disabled && 'btn-disabled opacity-50 cursor-not-allowed',
      )}
    >
      {children}
    </button>
  );
}

Falsy values (false, null, undefined) are silently ignored. No more '' entries cluttering your class strings.

Inline styles — for truly dynamic values

Inline styles use a JavaScript object with camelCase properties. Use them for values that cannot be expressed as static classes — like values derived from user input or calculations:

// ✅ Good use of inline style — value is dynamic and not a preset
<div style={{ width: `${progress}%`, backgroundColor: color }}>
  …
</div>

// ❌ Bad use — this should be a class
<div style={{ fontWeight: 'bold', color: 'red' }}>
  …
</div>

Vex: "Inline styles for layout decisions? No. Inline styles for runtime values that can't be CSS variables? Yes. The boundary is: if you could write it in a stylesheet once and always use it, write it in a stylesheet."

Putting it together — the variant pattern

const VARIANT_CLASSES = {
  primary:   'bg-blue-600 text-white hover:bg-blue-700',
  secondary: 'bg-gray-100 text-gray-900 hover:bg-gray-200',
  danger:    'bg-red-600 text-white hover:bg-red-700',
};

function Button({ variant = 'primary', size = 'md', className, children, ...props }) {
  return (
    <button
      className={cn(
        'inline-flex items-center rounded font-medium transition-colors',
        size === 'sm' && 'px-3 py-1.5 text-sm',
        size === 'md' && 'px-4 py-2 text-base',
        size === 'lg' && 'px-6 py-3 text-lg',
        VARIANT_CLASSES[variant],
        className,  // allow callers to extend
      )}
      {...props}
    >
      {children}
    </button>
  );
}

storyBeats.text: Vex shows you a wall of dye pots — each labelled, each isolated. 'The old way was one giant pot,' she says. 'Every spell bled into every other. CSS Modules give each component its own pot.'

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: A className is just a prop. That means it's JavaScript — and JavaScript means logic. You can build class strings from state, from props, from anything. The cn() utility cleans up the mess: pass it anything truthy, and it builds the string for you.

storyBeats.speaker: Dynamic classes with cn()

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a <StatusBadge> component. It receives a status prop: 'active', 'inactive', or 'pending'.

  • Render a <span data-testid="badge">
  • Apply a base class "badge" always
  • Apply "badge-active" when status is 'active'
  • Apply "badge-inactive" when status is 'inactive'
  • Apply "badge-pending" when status is 'pending'
  • Render the status text as children (capitalised: Active / Inactive / Pending)

Implement cn() yourself as a small helper, or use template literals — your choice.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a <ProgressBar> component from scratch. Props: value (0–100), variant ('default' | 'success' | 'danger'). Render an outer track div and an inner fill div. The fill's width should be an inline style set to value%. The outer track always has class "progress-track"; the inner fill has "progress-fill" plus "progress-fill--success" or "progress-fill--danger" for those variants.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a junior developer why className can be dynamic in React when HTML's class attribute cannot. Then explain when you should use CSS Modules vs. a cn() utility with utility classes vs. inline styles — give one concrete example where each is the right tool.

questions.prompt: What is the primary benefit of CSS Modules over plain CSS files?
options: Class names are scoped to the component — they cannot accidentally clash with classes in other files
CSS Modules run faster than plain CSS because they are processed at runtime
CSS Modules allow you to write CSS-in-JS syntax inside a .css file
CSS Modules automatically add vendor prefixes for cross-browser support
questions.answer: Class names are scoped to the component — they cannot accidentally clash with classes in other files
questions.explanation: CSS Modules transform class names like `.card` into unique identifiers like `Card_card__x8Kp2` at build time. This prevents global namespace collisions — you can have a `.card` class in every component file without them interfering. It's a build-time scoping mechanism, not a runtime one.

questions.prompt: A Button component needs the class `btn` always, `btn-primary` if `variant='primary'`, and `btn-sm` if `size='sm'`. Which className expression is cleanest?
options: All three approaches produce identical output and the choice doesn't matter
questions.explanation: cn() is cleanest because falsy values (false, undefined, null) are silently dropped — no empty strings in the output. Option B produces `btn  ` with trailing spaces when conditions are false. Option C adds empty strings to the array. All three work but cn() stays clean and readable as conditions grow.

questions.prompt: When is an inline `style` prop the correct choice over a CSS class?
options: When the value is computed at runtime from user input or state — e.g. `style={{ width: progress + '%' }}`
When you want to ensure the style cannot be overridden by global CSS
When applying more than three styles at once, for performance
Inline styles should never be used in React — always use className
questions.answer: When the value is computed at runtime from user input or state — e.g. `style={{ width: progress + '%' }}`
questions.explanation: Inline styles are appropriate when the value cannot be predetermined — a progress bar width, a user-chosen colour, a calculated position. For fixed visual treatments (fonts, colours, spacing), use classes. Inline styles bypass the cascade and can't be overridden by utility classes, so they should be scoped to truly dynamic values.
